3. Theoretical Frameworks to Enhance Gen Z Engagement and Performance

The increasing diversity and complexity of the modern workforce necessitate the adoption of theoretical frameworks that cater to the unique needs and preferences of Gen Z employees. This section will explore two prominent theoretical frameworks that can enhance Gen Z engagement and performance: Self-Determination Theory (SDT) and Transformational Leadership.

1. Self-Determination Theory (SDT): A Multidimensional Approach to Enhancing Employee Motivation

Self-Determination Theory (SDT) posits that human behavior is motivated by three innate psychological needs: autonomy, competence, and relatedness (Deci & Ryan, 2000). By incorporating these principles into organizational design, managers can foster a work environment that promotes employee engagement and performance. Specifically, SDT suggests that autonomy can be enhanced through flexible work models and self-directed projects, allowing employees to take ownership of their work and develop a sense of control (Amabile, 1993). Competence can be fostered through opportunities for continual learning and skill development, enabling employees to grow professionally and feel a sense of accomplishment (Latham & Locke, 2002). Relatedness can be promoted through a supportive workplace culture that encourages collaboration, social interaction, and a sense of belonging (Cameron et al., 2006).

2. Transformational Leadership: A Catalyst for Gen Z Engagement and Performance

Transformational Leadership (TL) is a leadership style that emphasizes the importance of inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, and individualized consideration (Bass, 1985). TL leaders who articulate a compelling vision that resonates with Gen Z's values can inspire and motivate employees to work towards a common goal (House, 1977). Intellectual stimulation can be encouraged through innovation and critical thinking, allowing employees to develop new ideas and solutions (Amabile, 1993). Individualized consideration can be demonstrated through attention to individual developmental needs and career aspirations, enabling employees to grow professionally and feel valued (Eisenberger et al., 1986).
